days.reason: Matthew 8 is a central text for the 3rd Sunday in Lent. The chapter shows Jesus' power over sickness, death, nature, and demons, illustrating the struggle between God's kingdom and the power of evil. Especially the casting out of demons (vv. 28-34) and the calming of the storm (vv. 23-27) emphasize that Jesus is Lord over all that threatens humanity, a central theme for Lent.

The account of the officer's faith (vv. 5-13) is an example of 'faith without seeing' and boundless trust in God's word, which is a central theme for the 2nd Sunday in Lent (the struggle of faith and perseverance).
The call to total devotion and discipleship ('let the dead bury their own dead') emphasizes the requirement for repentance and prioritizing God's kingdom, which is central to Lent.

This chapter contains a series of healings (leper, officer's servant, Peter's mother-in-law, demon-possessed) that directly fulfill the prophecy in verse 17: 'He took our illnesses and bore our diseases'. This is a central theme for Shrove Sunday, which marks the transition into Lent and focuses on Jesus' suffering and his role as the suffering servant (Isaiah 53) who bears humanity's burdens.

The parable about the cost of discipleship ('the foxes have holes...') and the call to let the dead bury their own dead emphasize the requirement for total devotion and self-imposed sacrifice, which is central to Lent and preparation for Easter.
The account of the storm on the sea and Jesus' power over nature shows his divine sovereignty, an important theme in Lent to strengthen faith during trials.
The casting out of demons from the possessed in Gerasa shows the struggle between God's kingdom and evil, a theme often addressed in Lent as a time to choose sides and make room for God.

_versions.reason:
[major] There is an incorrect linking of the entire Matthew 8 to Shrove Sunday. Shrove Sunday marks the transition into Lent and often focuses on repentance and preparation, but the central theological theme in Matthew 8 is not primarily 'the suffering servant' or 'Lenten penitence', but rather **Jesus' divine power over sickness, death, nature, and demons** as well as **the nature of faith**. 

Especially verse 17 ('He took our illnesses...') is a fulfillment of prophecy, but this chapter is not the liturgical standard reading for Shrove Sunday. In many church years (e.g., Year A in the Church of Norway), this chapter is read on the **3rd Sunday in Lent** (Lent-3) or **2nd Sunday in Lent** (Lent-2) depending on the year, but most naturally as a chapter about **faith and the power of God's kingdom**, often linked to **Lent-3** (the struggle against evil) or **Lent-2** (perseverance in faith). 

Furthermore, it is incorrect to call this 'primary' for Shrove Sunday. Shrove Sunday often has texts about repentance (e.g., Luke 15 or similar). Linking the entire chapter to Shrove Sunday is a liturgical error.; [major] Matthew 8 is a classic text for **the 3rd Sunday in Lent (Lent-3)**. The theme 'The struggle between God's kingdom and the power of evil' (exorcisms, healings, the storm) fits perfectly with the liturgy for this Sunday. Verses 28-34 (Gerasa) are especially central to this theme. It should be a 'primary' tag for Lent-3.; [minor] Parts of the chapter (especially verses 5-13 about the officer's faith and verses 19-22 about discipleship) can also be linked to **the 2nd Sunday in Lent (Lent-2)**, which deals with 'The struggle of faith and perseverance'. But Lent-3 is the stronger link for the entire chapter.; [major] Although one could argue for a weak link to Shrove Sunday via the 'suffering servant' theme in verse 17, it is not strong enough to justify 'primary' or even 'secondary' for the whole chapter. It is a liturgical error to use this chapter as the main text for Shrove Sunday.
